beliefs.practice: Reuse a single MongoClient (pymongo.MongoClient) across the app process and do not create a new client per request; rely on the client's built-in connection pooling and set sensible maxPoolSize and serverSelectionTimeoutMS.

Never store the DocumentDB/Cosmos connection string or primary keys in source control or plaintext files; read them from environment variables at runtime and, in production, keep them in Azure Key Vault and inject via environment or secret store.

Use the least-privilege credentials for runtime operations: avoid using the account primary key in app code; prefer per-application credentials, resource tokens, or managed identities/role-based auth where the Mongo/Cosmos API supports them.
Model documents to include a dedicated patientId field and use that as the query filter for access control, and (when appropriate) as the partition key to limit RU cost and ensure efficient lookups.

Choose the collection partition key carefully: pick a high-cardinality, evenly-distributed key (often patientId for per-patient isolation) so queries scoped to a patient target a single partition and avoid fanout across many partitions.

Store embeddings as a numeric array field (e.g., embedding: [float,...]) and keep the original chunk text and metadata (source id, offsets) in separate fields so responses can include grounded citations.

When creating a vector (cosmosSearch) index, ensure the index configuration matches the embedding dimensionality (e.g., 1536) and algorithm parameters (HNSW/IVF, metric) to avoid mismatches and failures.

Pre-filter vector KNN searches by patientId (or partition key) in the same query so the vector search only considers that patient's documents; do not rely on application-side filtering after fetching neighbors.
Use parameterized queries / structured query builders for Mongo-style queries (no string-concatenated filters) to avoid injection risks and ensure correct query shapes for the server to optimize.

Implement transient-fault handling: wrap database operations with retries using exponential backoff, respect idempotency (do not blindly retry non-idempotent writes), and pay attention to 429 (RequestRateTooLarge) responses to back off.

Monitor and budget Request Units (RUs): instrument queries (including vector KNN queries) to measure RU consumption, and provision or autoscale throughput to cover peak vector search workloads and index builds.

Do not log PHI (patient identifiers, clinical text, embeddings) to logs or error traces. Mask or redact patient-identifying fields in any logs, and ensure logging configuration is safe for healthcare data.
Use network isolation: restrict cluster traffic with IP firewall rules, VNet/private endpoints, and avoid exposing the cluster to the public internet whenever possible.
Enable encryption at rest (managed by Azure) and ensure TLS is enforced for connections; validate TLS server certs on the client and require TLS 1.2+.

When creating indexes in production, prefer non-blocking/background index builds or schedule index creation during maintenance windows because large index builds (especially vector indexes) can consume CPU, memory, and RUs.

Use schema validation or application-side validation to ensure required fields (patientId, chunkId, embedding, text, source) exist and embeddings have the expected dimensionality before inserting documents.

Keep vector index metadata (algorithm, dimensions, metric) and client embedding pre-processing (normalization) in source control or config so embeddings generated at ingest time match the index assumptions.

Prefer storing chunk-level provenance (document id, chunk offsets, page numbers) and include stable identifiers so returned summaries can reference exact source text for auditability and clinician verification.
Be conservative with index scope: only index fields required for queries and vector search; avoid creating unnecessary indexes that waste RU and storage and can slow writes.
Test index creation and vector queries against a staging copy of the dataset and validate query plans and explain output (via explain() or provider tooling) before applying to production.

When using the MongoDB-compatible protocol against Cosmos/DocumentDB, prefer tooling and commands compatible with the provider; if a management tool fails to create a specialized index (like vector/cosmosSearch), use the provider-recommended runCommand or REST/portal APIs with proper privileges.
Ensure patient-level authorization is enforced at the application layer in addition to DB filters: verify the authenticated user is allowed to read a given patientId before issuing database queries.
Set sensible read/write timeouts and limit the number of returned documents for KNN queries (request top-k and return pre-specified fields) to reduce RU usage and avoid returning large payloads.
Rotate and revoke keys promptly on personnel changes or suspected compromise; audit key usage and use separate keys for dev/staging/production environments.
